newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia watching yen, Japan rates for exports boost.
newsitem.headline: Asia watching yen, Japan rates for exports boost.

text.p: Asian nations are watching the yen and Japanese interest rates closely for signs of a monetary tightening, which would provide a welcome boost to an expected rebound in Asian exports next year, economists say.
"Right now, it's a little too premature to call," Paul Alapat, economist at Lehman Brothers in Hong Kong said on Thursday.

"But if there is a sustained tightening of the yen that means the U.S. dollar will come off and will have some impact on regional exports. But we have to wait to see how the Japanese economy recovers and if Japanese interest rates are hiked."

The U.S. dollar sank almost two yen on Thursday, reaching 111.27 during the overnight session, after a Japanese ministry of finance official, Eisuke Sakakibara, signalled earlier in the day that the long slide in the yen had gone far enough.
The dollar recovered to about 112.24/112.31 yen at midday Friday.

A possible shift in Japanese monetary policy would be very significant for Asian exports, which have suffered from a U.S. dollar now 40 percent stronger than its record post-war low of 79.95 yen, reached in April 1995.
Many Asian nations link their currencies to the U.S. dollar or a basket of currencies heavily-weighted in favour of the U.S. dollar.

A weaker U.S. dollar would make many Asian exports cheaper and more competitive, and help to counter regional export weakness caused this year by a global inventory correction and, in some cases, tighter domestic monetary policy.
"It typically means that Asian exports are now more competitive with respect to products from Japan," Alapat said.
This is particularly significant for South Korea, whose products compete head-to-head with Japanese exports but whose won has failed to keep pace with the yen's depreciation.

A stronger yen could compromise South Korea's competitiveness against Japan, but it could also cause some easing of South Korean interest rates, which were kept high to counter the effects of South Korea's own currency depreciation policy, said Marshall Mays, chief strategist at Nikko Research Centre (Hong Kong) Ltd.
"One way or another, Koreans will no longer have any incentive to keep interest rates so high," he said.

But Alapat said it typically took six to 12 months for a shift in currency policy to affect export performance, and said the movements by the yen so far were insufficient to provide a significant short-term boost.
"The main point to keep in mind is we're talking about one day's movements on certain comments. We don't have any fundamental change as yet," Alapat said.

"Right now, dollar-yen is still holding above 110. If it starts breaking 105 and goes significantly below that (it would be helpful) but at this point, we've only seen side fluctuations both ways. It's too early to call a fundamnental reversal."

Mays joined other commentators who noted the timing of Thursday's remarks from Sakakibara, which came just one day after the U.S. election. The United States is widely expected to become much tougher in trade issues.
"The people who paid for this election will not want the Japanese with these low exchange rates," Mays said.

"You can guarantee the Americans will start getting tough with the Koreans and the Japanese. They'll say to Korea, 'We know you're suppressing your currency, stop it. And you just joined the OECD (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development).'"
